- Overestimate prices after recent spikes, especially when sentiment is positive or neutral (e.g., >0.30); model tends to overshoot and fail to correct downward.
- Underestimate prices during prolonged downward trends or negative sentiment (e.g., <0.10), especially if recent prices are falling; model fails to recognize mean reversion.
- When sentiment is high (e.g., >0.70) and prices are rising, model often overreacts with exaggerated upward bias; reduce forecast slope or add downward drag.
- If sentiment is low and prices are stable or slightly falling, model tends to underestimate further decline; adjust forecast downward by 2–5% of recent range.
- For 30-day horizon, model often overestimates early in the forecast window (first 5–7 days) — apply a “lag correction” by reducing first 5 days’ forecast by 1–3% relative to history.
- When sentiment is volatile (rapid swings >0.50), model overfits short-term noise; smooth forecast by averaging 3–5 prior days’ values or dampen sentiment-driven spikes.
- If true outcome is significantly below forecast (e.g., >10% deviation), check if sentiment was high recently — if so, reduce forecast by 5–10% to account for sentiment-driven overconfidence.
- If true outcome is significantly above forecast (e.g., >10% deviation), check if sentiment was low — if so, increase forecast by 5–10% to account for sentiment-driven underreaction.
